claim: ATM protein kinase regulates the DNA damage response (DDR) and is associated with cancer suppression.
source: Ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein kinase regulates the DNA damage response (DDR) and is associated with cancer suppression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge about ATM's role.

claim: ATM depletion in metastatic cancer cells reduced cell migration and invasion.
source: ATM depletion in metastatic cancer cells reduced cell migration and invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: IL-8 expression required ATM and was regulated by oxidative stress.
source: IL-8 expression required ATM and was regulated by oxidative stress.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: IL-8 addition rescued cell migration and invasion defects in ATM-depleted cells.
source: IL-8 was validated as an ATM target by its ability to rescue cell migration and invasion defects in ATM-depleted cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5F,G.

claim: ATM-depletion in human breast cancer cells reduced lung tumors in a mouse xenograft model.
source: Finally, ATM-depletion in human breast cancer cells reduced lung tumors in a mouse xenograft model and clinical data validated IL-8 in lung metastasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Clinical data validated IL-8 in lung metastasis.
source: Finally, ATM-depletion in human breast cancer cells reduced lung tumors in a mouse xenograft model and clinical data validated IL-8 in lung metastasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by patient data analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: DNA damaging agents (ionizing radiation, etoposide, doxorubicin) had little effect on cell migration in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: DNA damage, including ionizing radiation (IR), topoisomerase II poisons etoposide (Et) and doxorubicin (Dox), had little effect on cell migration in the highly metastatic human breast cancer cell line MDA-MB-231 as measured by wound healing assays (Figure 1A, quantified in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: DNA damaging treatments arrested the cell cycle and inhibited proliferation in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: These treatments arrested the cell cycle and inhibited proliferation (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Cell migration is independent from DSB induction by DNA damaging agents, as well as cell cycle and growth arrest.
source: Thus, cell migration is independent from DSB induction by DNA damaging agents, as well as cell cycle and growth arrest.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that DNA damage arrests cells but doesn't affect migration.

claim: ATM depletion reduced cell migration in the presence or absence of IR-induced damage.
source: Strikingly, ATM depletion reduced cell migration in the presence or absence of IR-induced damage (Figure 1E, quantified in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: ATM promotes cell migration and invasion in MDA-MB-231 cells in the absence of exogenous DNA damage.
source: Thus, ATM promotes cell migration and invasion in MDA-MB-231 cells in the absence of exogenous DNA damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing ATM's role in migration without DNA damage.

claim: Depletion of CHK2, MRE11 or NBS1 did not reduce cell migration.
source: In contrast to ATM inhibition, depletion of CHK2, MRE11 or NBS1 did not reduce cell migration, suggesting ATM-mediated cell migration occurred independently of DSB-dependent ATM activation (Figure 2A,B; depletion analysis shown in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: ATM-mediated cell migration occurred independently of DSB-dependent ATM activation.
source: In contrast to ATM inhibition, depletion of CHK2, MRE11 or NBS1 did not reduce cell migration, suggesting ATM-mediated cell migration occurred independently of DSB-dependent ATM activation (Figure 2A,B; depletion analysis shown in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that DSB signaling components don't affect migration.

claim: Chemical inhibition of oxidative stress using N-acetylcysteine (NAC) reduced cell migration similarly as depletion of ATM.
source: In support of this idea, chemical inhibition of oxidative stress in MDA-MB-231 cells using the reducing agent N-acetylcysteine (NAC) reduced cell migration similarly as depletion of ATM (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: NAC treatment inhibits intracellular oxidative stress.
source: We also showed that NAC treatment inhibits intracellular oxidative stress (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: NAC treatment reduced cell motility compared with control cells.
source: To rule out any influence of proliferation on cell migration in our analyses, we performed live-cell imaging to track the migration of individual cells. We found reduced cell motility in cells treated with NAC compared with control cells (Figure 2F,G and Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F,G and Videos 1, 2.

claim: ATM, independent from DSB signaling, promotes cell migration.
source: These data suggest that ATM, independent from DSB signaling, promotes cell migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing NAC and ATM depletion have similar effects.

claim: p53 is phosphorylated by ATM after oxidative stress.
source: However, p53 is phosphorylated by ATM after oxidative stress and mutant p53 is involved in TGFβ-dependent cell migration in MDA-MB-231 cells (Adorno et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mutant p53 is involved in TGFβ-dependent cell migration in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: However, p53 is phosphorylated by ATM after oxidative stress and mutant p53 is involved in TGFβ-dependent cell migration in MDA-MB-231 cells (Adorno et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of mutant p53 resulted in reduced cell migration.
source: As expected, inhibition of mutant p53 resulted in reduced cell migration (Figure 3A, quantified in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Co-depletion of ATM and mutant p53 resulted in a similar reduction of cell migration as either single gene knockdown alone.
source: Interestingly, co-depletion of ATM and mutant p53 resulted in a similar reduction of cell migration as either single gene knockdown alone (Figure 3A, quantified in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Mutant p53 depletion mildly reduced proliferation.
source: Although mutant p53 depletion mildly reduced proliferation, co-depletion of ATM resulted in an epistatic reduction of cell migration and invasion (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Co-depletion of ATM and mutant p53 resulted in an epistatic reduction of cell migration and invasion.
source: Although mutant p53 depletion mildly reduced proliferation, co-depletion of ATM resulted in an epistatic reduction of cell migration and invasion (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ATM and mutant p53 are required for the cell migration and invasion phenotypes observed in highly invasive cancer cell lines.
source: Taken together, these results from multiple human cancer cell lines suggest that ATM and mutant p53 are required for the cell migration and invasion phenotypes observed in these highly invasive cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments in MDA-MB-231 and BT-549 cells.

claim: Out of hundreds of genes in ATM-depleted cells whose mRNA levels were differentially regulated more than 1.5-fold, only ~40 genes showed equivalent regulation between siATM and si mutant p53 cells.
source: Out of the hundreds of genes in ATM-depleted cells whose mRNA levels were differentially regulated more than 1.5-fold compared to control siNon-coding (siNC) cells, only ∼40 genes showed equivalent regulation between siATM and si mutant p53 cells (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A and supplementary files.

claim: Gene ontology analysis indicated that genes involved in the response to wound healing, including cell migration genes, were in the top 10 GO categories for both ATM and mutant p53 depleted samples.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis indicated that genes involved in the response to wound healing, including cell migration genes, were in the top 10 GO categories for both ATM and mutant p53 depleted samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: GO analysis of genes co-regulated by ATM and mutant p53 identified almost exclusively pathways involving cell migration.
source: GO analysis of genes co-regulated by ATM and mutant p53 identified almost exclusively pathways involving cell migration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1C) in agreement with our data showing reduced migration in ATM or mutant p53 deficient cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The inflammatory cytokine interleukin-8 (IL-8) was the most down-regulated gene in both siATM and si mutant p53 cells.
source: Interestingly, the inflammatory cytokine interleukin-8 (IL-8) was the most down-regulated gene in both siATM and si mutant p53 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Depletion of ATM in cancer cell lines containing WT p53 resulted in increased IL-8 mRNA levels.
source: Conversely, depletion of ATM in cancer cell lines containing WT p53 resulted in increased IL-8 mRNA levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: ATM promotes IL-8 levels in the context of mutant p53.
source: These results suggest that ATM promotes IL-8 levels in the context of mutant p53.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of ATM depletion in mutant vs WT p53 cells.

claim: IL-8 is upregulated in several cancers, including breast cancer, where it mediates several cancer promoting pathways including cell migration.
source: IL-8 is upregulated in several cancers, including breast cancer, where it mediates several cancer promoting pathways including cell migration (Campbell et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The IL-8 promoter contains many transcription factor binding sites, including NF-κB, which regulates IL-8 expression.
source: The IL-8 promoter contains many transcription factor binding sites, including NF-κB, which regulates IL-8 expression and is linked to the DDR through ATM activation by DSBs (Mukaida et al., 1990; Biton and Ashkenazi, 2011; McCool and Miyamoto, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ~90% of IL-8 promoter activity was lost by mutating the NF-κB binding site.
source: We confirmed IL-8 promoter regulation by NF-κB as ∼90% of IL-8 promoter activity was lost by mutating the NF-κB binding site (mut IL-8, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Depletion of ATM or mutant p53 reduced IL-8 promoter activity similarly as mut IL-8.
source: Interestingly, depletion of ATM or mutant p53 reduced IL-8 promoter activity similarly as mut IL-8, showing ATM regulation of IL-8 occurs at the transcriptional level (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ATM regulation of IL-8 occurs at the transcriptional level.
source: Interestingly, depletion of ATM or mutant p53 reduced IL-8 promoter activity similarly as mut IL-8, showing ATM regulation of IL-8 occurs at the transcriptional level (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the promoter activity assay results.

claim: Depletion of NF-κB p65 or NEMO abrogated IL-8 expression in MDA-MB-231.
source: As expected, we observed that depletion of NF-κB p65, a subunit of NF-κB dimer, or NEMO abrogated IL-8 expression in MDA-MB-231 (Figure 4E, Freund et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4E, with citation support.

claim: Reduced levels of ATM or mutant p53 impaired NF-κB accumulation on the IL-8 promoter.
source: ChIP analyses revealed that reduced levels of ATM or mutant p53 impaired NF-κB accumulation on the IL-8 promoter (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: ATM and mutant p53 are required for NF-κB activity, which is necessary to regulate IL-8 expression.
source: Collectively, our results strongly suggest that ATM and mutant p53 are required for NF-κB activity, which is necessary to regulate IL-8 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing the relationship between ATM, p53, NF-κB and IL-8.

claim: IL-8 depletion reduced cell migration and invasion.
source: Further analyses supported the notion of IL-8 as the gene responsible for reduced migration in ATM-depleted MDA-MB-231 cells as (1) IL-8 depletion reduced cell migration and invasion, (2) NAC treatment reduced IL-8 mRNA levels and (3) oxidative stress induction by H2O2 increased IL-8 levels and (4) H2O2-induced IL-8 expression was dependent on ATM (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: NAC treatment reduced IL-8 mRNA levels.
source: Further analyses supported the notion of IL-8 as the gene responsible for reduced migration in ATM-depleted MDA-MB-231 cells as (1) IL-8 depletion reduced cell migration and invasion, (2) NAC treatment reduced IL-8 mRNA levels and (3) oxidative stress induction by H2O2 increased IL-8 levels and (4) H2O2-induced IL-8 expression was dependent on ATM (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Oxidative stress induction by H2O2 increased IL-8 levels.
source: Further analyses supported the notion of IL-8 as the gene responsible for reduced migration in ATM-depleted MDA-MB-231 cells as (1) IL-8 depletion reduced cell migration and invasion, (2) NAC treatment reduced IL-8 mRNA levels and (3) oxidative stress induction by H2O2 increased IL-8 levels and (4) H2O2-induced IL-8 expression was dependent on ATM (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: H2O2-induced IL-8 expression was dependent on ATM.
source: Further analyses supported the notion of IL-8 as the gene responsible for reduced migration in ATM-depleted MDA-MB-231 cells as (1) IL-8 depletion reduced cell migration and invasion, (2) NAC treatment reduced IL-8 mRNA levels and (3) oxidative stress induction by H2O2 increased IL-8 levels and (4) H2O2-induced IL-8 expression was dependent on ATM (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ATM regulates a transcriptional network that includes the NF-κB-regulated gene IL-8.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that ATM regulates a transcriptional network that includes the NF-κB-regulated gene IL-8.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression and mechanistic studies.

claim: The ATM pathway promotes cell migration and invasion in MDA-MB-231 cells through a cell intrinsic mechanism that is reliant on endogenous oxidative stress.
source: Our data suggests that this ATM pathway promotes cell migration and invasion in MDA-MB-231 cells through a cell intrinsic mechanism that is reliant on endogenous oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NAC and H2O2 experiments.

claim: The addition of recombinant IL-8 rescued both migration and invasion properties in both mutant p53 and ATM-depleted cells.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the addition of recombinant IL-8 rescued both migration and invasion properties in both mutant p53 and ATM-depleted cells (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: IL-8 is an ATM regulated gene target that strongly influences the reduced migration and invasion of ATM and mutant p53 deficient MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells.
source: These data identify IL-8 as an ATM regulated gene target that strongly influences the reduced migration and invasion of ATM and mutant p53 deficient MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with recombinant IL-8.

claim: ATM is considered a tumor suppressor as its deletion in mice results in tumors.
source: ATM is considered a tumor suppressor as its deletion in mice results in tumors, patients with mutations in ATM in the human disorder Ataxia telangiectasia have increased cancer risks, and several hematological cancers have been reported to express defective ATM (Cremona and Behrens, 2013; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013; Stracker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Patients with mutations in ATM in the human disorder Ataxia telangiectasia have increased cancer risks.
source: ATM is considered a tumor suppressor as its deletion in mice results in tumors, patients with mutations in ATM in the human disorder Ataxia telangiectasia have increased cancer risks, and several hematological cancers have been reported to express defective ATM (Cremona and Behrens, 2013; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013; Stracker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Several hematological cancers have been reported to express defective ATM.
source: ATM is considered a tumor suppressor as its deletion in mice results in tumors, patients with mutations in ATM in the human disorder Ataxia telangiectasia have increased cancer risks, and several hematological cancers have been reported to express defective ATM (Cremona and Behrens, 2013; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013; Stracker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increased levels of IL-8 are associated with the metastatic potential of several cancer types, including colon cancer and melanoma.
source: However, our identification for a requirement of ATM to promote IL-8 expression, cell migration and invasion in vitro, as well as the association of increased levels of IL-8 with the metastatic potential of several cancer types, including colon cancer and melanoma (Lee et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012), prompted us to evaluate if ATM could influence tumorigenesis and promote pro-metastatic processes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: shATM and shNC cells exhibited similar cellular morphology and growth rates in vitro.
source: shATM and shNC cells exhibited similar cellular morphology and growth rates in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B) and shATM cells exhibited reduced cell migration and invasion, as well as reduced IL8 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: shATM cells exhibited reduced cell migration and invasion, as well as reduced IL8 expression.
source: shATM and shNC cells exhibited similar cellular morphology and growth rates in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B) and shATM cells exhibited reduced cell migration and invasion, as well as reduced IL8 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Both shATM and shNC cells formed colonies with similar efficiency in soft agar.
source: In addition, both shATM and shNC cells formed colonies with similar efficiency in soft agar (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: ATM depletion by shRNA did not overtly alter the growth properties of MDA-MB0231 cells.
source: Thus, ATM depletion by shRNA did not overtly alter the growth properties of MDA-MB0231 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the soft agar and growth rate experiments.

claim: ATM-depletion increased primary tumor growth in orthotopic injections.
source: To examine the influence of ATM on tumor growth in vivo, we then orthotopically injected these cells into the mammary fat pad. There, we observed an increase in primary tumor growth, consistent with the well-established role of ATM in tumor suppression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Lung colonization was strongly suppressed in cells with reduced ATM levels compared to control cells.
source: To address whether ATM depletion could influence the ability of these cells to colonize secondary sites, we performed tail vein injections with shATM and shNC MDA-MB 231 cells and assessed lung colonization after 9 weeks. In contrast to the pro-tumorigenic effects of ATM depletion on primary growth, lung colonization was strongly suppressed in cells with reduced ATM levels compared to control cells (Figure 6D,E), consistent with the ability of ATM activity to regulate IL-8 mediated cell migration and invasion capacity.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: The expression of IL-8 was significantly associated with metastasis to the lung but not bone or brain.
source: To examine the relationship between ATM and IL-8 expression and metastasis in human breast cancer, we analyzed a set of expression arrays from 560 breast cancer patients with clinical annotation (Morales et al., 2014). The expression of IL-8 was significantly associated with metastasis to the lung but not bone or brain (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: IL-8, and potentially ATM, do not affect all metastatic processes similarly in all tissues.
source: These data suggest that IL-8, and potentially ATM, do not affect all metastatic processes similarly in all tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue-specific association of IL-8 with metastasis.

claim: ATM serves as a tumor suppressor to limit the proliferation or survival of cancer cells during primary tumor formation.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that ATM can play dual functions in breast cancer tumor progression. On the one hand, ATM serves as a tumor suppressor to limit the proliferation or survival of cancer cells during primary tumor formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the orthotopic tumor growth experiments.

claim: ATM can promote pro-metastatic processes such as lung colonization.
source: However, based on our findings, ATM can also promote pro-metastatic processes such as lung colonization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tail vein injection experiments.

claim: ATM functions in tumor progression are likely through its ability to control the transcription of key regulators, including IL-8, that promote cell migration and invasion to influence metastatic colonization.
source: These functions of ATM are likely through its ability to control the transcription of key regulators, including IL-8, that promote cell migration and invasion to influence metastatic colonization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo experiments.

claim: ATM is known to regulate several pro-inflammatory cytokines as part of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) in senescent cells.
source: ATM is known to regulate several pro-inflammatory cytokines as part of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) in senescent cells (Rodier et al., 2009; Coppe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The SASP can be mediated by DNA damage induced ATM signaling through MRN and CHK2, but not p53.
source: The SASP can be mediated by DNA damage induced ATM signaling through MRN and CHK2, but not p53.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: A role for p38 MAPK in the SASP has been defined that is independent of the initial ATM-dependent damage response.
source: In addition, a role for p38 MAPK in the SASP has been defined that is independent of the initial ATM-dependent damage response (Freund et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Senescent cells are thought to promote tumor progression in the microenvironment through paracrine signaling by secreted pro-inflammatory factors including cytokines.
source: Senescent cells are thought to promote tumor progression in the microenvironment through paracrine signaling by secreted pro-inflammatory factors including cytokines (Coppe et al., 2008, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ATM has been shown to regulate IL-8 secretion in response to DSB formation by etoposide, which is dependent on NF-κB and NEMO but independent from p53.
source: ATM has also been shown to regulate IL-8 secretion in response to DSB formation by etoposide, which is dependent on NF-κB and NEMO but independent from p53 (Biton and Ashkenazi., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ATM, through a pathway requiring mutant p53, can support a transcriptional program that includes several pro-metastatic genes including IL-8 that maintain cell migration and invasion.
source: From our data, we conclude that ATM, through a pathway requiring mutant p53, can support a transcriptional program that includes several pro-metastatic genes including IL-8 that maintain cell migration and invasion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: A recent study identified a fundamentally different type of anti-cancer pathway mediated by ATM in a MLL-AF9 driven acute myeloid leukemia model.
source: Interestingly, a recent study identified a fundamentally different type of anti-cancer pathway mediated by ATM in a MLL-AF9 driven acute myeloid leukemia model (Santos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the MLL-AF9 leukemia model, ATM was required to block the differentiation capacity of cells, thereby promoting their tumorigenic properties.
source: In this instance, ATM was required to block the differentiation capacity of these cells, thereby promoting their tumorigenic properties.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a cited study.

claim: p38 MAPK plays both pro and anti-tumorigenic roles.
source: p38 MAPK plays both pro and anti-tumorigenic roles and its downregulation has been demonstrated to reduce tumor growth and survival but also to promote the metastasis of colorectal cancer to the lung through the modulation of inflammatory responses (Gupta et al., 2014; Urosevic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Downregulation of p38 MAPK has been demonstrated to reduce tumor growth and survival but also to promote the metastasis of colorectal cancer to the lung through the modulation of inflammatory responses.
source: p38 MAPK plays both pro and anti-tumorigenic roles and its downregulation has been demonstrated to reduce tumor growth and survival but also to promote the metastasis of colorectal cancer to the lung through the modulation of inflammatory responses (Gupta et al., 2014; Urosevic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ATM represents another DDR factor that, like p53 or p38, can differentially influence pathways relevant to diverse aspects of tumorigenesis in a context dependent manner.
source: Thus, emerging evidence indicates that ATM represents another DDR factor that, like p53 or p38, can differentially influence pathways relevant to diverse aspects of tumorigenesis in a context dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and comparison with other factors.

claim: Comparative expression analysis revealed wound healing as a major pathway regulated by both ATM and mutant p53.
source: Comparative expression analysis revealed wound healing as a major pathway regulated by both ATM and mutant p53.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the microarray analysis.

claim: Several pro-metastatic genes from the analysis in addition to IL-8, including CXCL11, CCL2, MMP1 and SAA2, were identified.
source: Several pro-metastatic genes from this analysis in addition to IL-8, including CXCL11, CCL2, MMP1 and SAA2, were identified.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the microarray analysis.

claim: Identifying IL-8 as a target of oxidative stress and ATM provides a link between activated ATM by oxidative stress and pro-metastatic pathways operating in cancer cells.
source: By identifying IL-8 as a target of oxidative stress and ATM, we provide a link between activated ATM by oxidative stress and pro-metastatic pathways operating in cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The results provide additional insights into other disease pathways involving ATM including angiogenesis, a pathway triggered by oxidative stress and dependent on IL-8.
source: Our results provide additional insights into other disease pathways involving ATM including angiogenesis, a pathway triggered by oxidative stress and dependent on IL-8 (Koch et al., 1992; Okuno et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Inhibitors of the IL-8 pathway are actively being developed and evaluated in pre-clinical studies and clinical trials for cancer and inflammatory diseases.
source: Inhibitors of the IL-8 pathway are actively being developed and evaluated in pre-clinical studies and clinical trials for cancer and inflammatory diseases (Waugh and Wilson, 2008; Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The work provides a rationale for evaluating the clinical efficacy of IL-8 inhibition in the context of lung metastasis.
source: Our work provides a rationale for evaluating the clinical efficacy of IL-8 inhibition in the context of lung metastasis, including the use of ATM inhibitors beyond their ability to radio-sensitize cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: High IL-8 expression levels in breast cancers were specifically correlated with lung metastasis.
source: It is intriguing that high IL-8 expression levels in breast cancers were specifically correlated with lung metastasis, a tissue location with high oxygen burden (Rosanna and Salvatore, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the patient data analysis.

claim: Regulation of IL-8 by ATM could promote a metastatic program that is important in an organ-specific context where oxidative stress and cytokine secretion occur.
source: Thus, regulation of IL-8 by ATM could promote a metastatic program that is important in an organ-specific context where oxidative stress and cytokine secretion occur.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the study's findings.

claim: Targeting ATM could inhibit IL-8 dependent processes involving tumor progression and metastasis in certain cancers.
source: We hypothesize based on our findings that targeting ATM could inhibit IL-8 dependent processes involving tumor progression and metastasis in certain cancers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the study's findings.

claim: ATM inhibition could be efficacious in the setting of other diseases involving oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory cytokines including inflammation, angiogenesis and aging.
source: In addition, based on our study and those of others, ATM inhibition could also be efficacious in the setting of other diseases involving oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory cytokines including inflammation, angiogenesis and aging (Osorio et al., 2012; Okuno et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the study's findings and cited work.

claim: DSBs activate ATM through interactions with the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) complex.
source: DSBs activate ATM through interactions with the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the results section.

claim: ATM phosphorylates many targets, including the effector kinase CHK2, which collectively orchestrate the DDR.
source: ATM phosphorylates many targets, including the effector kinase CHK2, which collectively orchestrate the DDR (Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003; Lee and Paull, 2005; Matsuoka et al., 2007; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ATM is activated by oxidative stress independently of DSBs, MRN or CHK2.
source: ATM is also activated by oxidative stress independently of DSBs, MRN or CHK2 (Guo et al., 2010), although the downstream pathways reliant on this ATM activation are unclear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The downstream pathways reliant on ATM activation by oxidative stress are unclear.
source: ATM is also activated by oxidative stress independently of DSBs, MRN or CHK2 (Guo et al., 2010), although the downstream pathways reliant on this ATM activation are unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the results section.

claim: Cancer treatments rely heavily on DNA damaging agents, including radiation and chemotherapeutics, to eliminate cancer cells and decrease tumor burden.
source: Cancer treatments rely heavily on DNA damaging agents, including radiation and chemotherapeutics, to eliminate cancer cells and decrease tumor burden (Begg et al., 2011; Lord and Ashworth, 2012; Cheung-Ong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DNA damaging cancer therapies activate complex signaling networks, termed the DNA damage response (DDR), that detect and signal the presence of DNA damage to promote cell cycle arrest and DNA repair.
source: These cancer therapies activate complex signaling networks, termed the DNA damage response (DDR), that detect and signal the presence of DNA damage to promote cell cycle arrest and DNA repair (Jackson and Bartek, 2009; Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ATM initiates a large signaling cascade in response to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) by phosphorylating many key proteins, including the tumor suppressor p53, to orchestrate the DDR.
source: The apical protein kinase ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) initiates a large signaling cascade in response to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) by phosphorylating many key proteins, including the tumor suppressor p53, to orchestrate the DDR (Shiloh and Ziv, 2013; Stracker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The DDR regulates cell fate decision pathways including apoptosis, senescence and differentiation.
source: The DDR regulates cell fate decision pathways including apoptosis, senescence and differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Many DDR pathways depend on ATM and/or p53 to enforce tumor suppressive anti-cancer barriers to limit proliferation in response to, and in the presence of, DNA damage.
source: Many of these pathways depend on ATM and/or p53 to enforce tumor suppressive anti-cancer barriers to limit proliferation in response to, and in the presence of, DNA damage (Norbury and Zhivotovsky, 2004; Bartkova et al., 2005; Gorgoulis et al., 2005; Bartkova et al., 2006; Di Micco et al., 2006; Vousden and Lane, 2007; Sherman et al., 2011; Roos and Kaina, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cancer cells exhibit genome instability.
source: However, cancer cells exhibit genome instability (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011) and often contain endogenous oxidative and replicative damage that can promote genetic alterations to drive malignant transformation (Klaunig et al., 2010; Hills and Diffley, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cancer cells often contain endogenous oxidative and replicative damage that can promote genetic alterations to drive malignant transformation.
source: However, cancer cells exhibit genome instability (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011) and often contain endogenous oxidative and replicative damage that can promote genetic alterations to drive malignant transformation (Klaunig et al., 2010; Hills and Diffley, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cancer cells evolve a defective DDR to allow cell proliferation in the presence of DNA damage, furthering genome instability and cancer progression.

claim: Defects in the DDR can profoundly influence DNA damage-dependent therapies both positively and negatively.
source: Defects in the DDR can also profoundly influence DNA damage-dependent therapies both positively and negatively (Bouwman and Jonkers, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: p53 is normally activated by stress signals and promotes tumor suppressor pathways.
source: This concept is perhaps best exemplified by p53, which is normally activated by stress signals and promotes tumor suppressor pathways (Bieging et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Tumor-associated gain-of-function p53 mutations that are most commonly observed in human cancers exhibit several tumor-promoting functions.
source: However, the tumor-associated gain-of-function p53 mutations that are most commonly observed in human cancers exhibit several tumor-promoting functions (Muller and Vousden, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Tumor suppressive or promoting activities from the same protein can be dictated by many factors including mutations, cell type, and/or disease context.
source: Thus, tumor suppressive or promoting activities from the same protein can be dictated by many factors including mutations, cell type, and/or disease context.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the introduction.

claim: ATM regulates complex signaling networks that are involved in many biological processes in addition to DSB signaling and repair.
source: ATM regulates complex signaling networks that are involved in many biological processes in addition to DSB signaling and repair (Stracker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Aside from increased tumorigenesis, ATM-deficiency results in altered metabolism, aberrant immune and inflammatory responses and increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Aside from increased tumorigenesis, ATM-deficiency results in altered metabolism, aberrant immune and inflammatory responses and increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS, Schneider et al., 2006; Alexander et al., 2010; Freund et al., 2011; Kulinski et al., 2012; Valentin-Vega et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Several of the pathological outcomes in ATM deficient mice have been linked to ROS and many of these pathologies can be reversed by the addition of antioxidants.
source: Several of the pathological outcomes in ATM deficient mice have been linked to ROS and many of these pathologies can be reversed by the addition of antioxidants, highlighting the important role of ATM in regulating redox-homeostasis (Ito et al., 2004; Reliene and Schiestl, 2006, 2007; Reliene et al., 2008; Freund et al., 2011; Okuno et al., 2012; D'Souza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ATM can be directly activated by ROS, independently from DSB signaling.
source: In addition, ATM can be directly activated by ROS, independently from DSB signaling, and has been implicated in mitochondrial quality control, potentially through an ability to localize to mitochondria (Guo et al., 2010; Valentin-Vega et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ATM has been implicated in mitochondrial quality control, potentially through an ability to localize to mitochondria.

claim: The substrates of ATM following ROS mediated activation, and how distinct they are from those modified following DNA damage, remains unknown.
source: The substrates of ATM following ROS mediated activation, and how distinct they are from those modified following DNA damage, remains unknown.

claim: The NF-κB family of transcription factors are activated by multiple stimuli that include DNA damage and ROS.

claim: NF-κB signaling regulates inflammation and is involved in cancer where it has been associated with both anti and pro-tumorigenic processes.

claim: NF-κB signaling can be regulated by ATM through the phosphorylation of NEMO, which aids in transmitting nuclear ATM signaling to activate NF-κB in the cytoplasm.

claim: Cancer cells acquire several capabilities in addition to uncontrolled proliferation during the multistep process of tumorigenesis, including cell migration and invasion that promote tumor metastasis.

claim: Metastasis occurs when a tumor spreads by means of cell migration and invasion to a secondary site, a process linked with the majority of cancer deaths.
source: Metastasis occurs when a tumor spreads by means of cell migration and invasion to a secondary site, a process linked with the majority of cancer deaths (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Several pathways suppress metastasis as part of tumor suppressive mechanisms.
source: Several pathways suppress this dangerous process as part of tumor suppressive mechanisms (Mehlen and Puisieux, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Increased genomic instability due to the acquisition of DDR defects has been proposed to play a role in the acquisition of metastatic traits based on human patient data.
source: Although the role of DNA damage and the DDR in this process has not been extensively explored experimentally, increased genomic instability due to the acquisition of DDR defects has been proposed to play a role in the acquisition of these traits based on human patient data (Halazonetis et al., 2008).
